opening.headline: Before launching an AI service for customers, we design who checks what and how to record it to complete the inspection.
body: The launch of an AI consulting service for customers is next week, but sometimes no one knows who checked what. The development team believes that the security team saw it, and the security team believes that the legal team saw it. In this situation, you won't even be able to tell which item is missing after the problem occurs.

In this class, we divide inspection items into four areas: policy, data, safety, and notice, and look at how to set approval entities that are distinct from inspectors and re-inspection conditions. Next, we explain cases where data items were empty and became a problem, and we summarize the criteria for determining completeness by finding blank spaces in the checklist.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Inspection items can be divided into policy, data, safety, and notice.
You can determine whether the inspection procedure has been completed

screens.title: Release without inspection procedures
screens.lead: Read about one team's situation ahead of launch. It is good to see where words of trust in each other become gaps in responsibility.

visual.alt: A scene where the three departments are connected by arrows pointing to each other, with the checklist in the middle empty.
labels: You must have seen it there, right?

paragraphs: AI consultation service for customers will be launched next week. The development team thinks the security team has checked, and the security team thinks the legal team has looked at the policy section. The legal team expects the development team to explain how the feature works.

No one lied, but no one checked the whole story. If something goes wrong after launch, you won't even know what items are missing or who was supposed to check them. It is not that there is no responsibility, but responsibility is scattered.

Pre-launch inspection procedures are a deterrent to this dispersion. It can be called a procedure only when the items to be checked, the person to be checked, and a record of what has been checked are all tied together in one set.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: At the end of this class, you will be able to tell which blank spaces on the team's checklist above are divided into four areas.

screens.outro: First, let's think about how our organization is doing.

screens.title: Who checks what before launch
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer, so first think about your organization and then click.

items.answer: If the people and items being checked are only in a person's head, they disappear when the person in charge changes. The starting point of the process is to document the items and responsibilities. Even if there are not many items, if the details of who is in charge are left out, the scattering of responsibilities we saw earlier will occur.

items.prompt: Is there a record of confirmation?
items.answer: “Confirmed” is not a record. There must be supporting documentation indicating what was seen and verified and the date of verification. Without records, it is impossible to prove that an inspection was performed after an accident.

items.prompt: Do I check again if the model or settings change?
items.answer: If you do one check right before launch and you're done, that check will only be for the model and settings on launch day. You must decide in advance whether to re-examine if any changes occur. This standard is a re-check condition.

screens.outro: Now that we have checked the current status, let's divide the inspection items into four areas.

screens.title: Four areas to check: policy, data, safety, and notification.
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the four areas you need to check before launch and the evidence you need to fill out for each area. Note that at the end of each area there is a space to write down the responsible department and supporting documents.

visual.alt: Illustration of a table where the release checklist is divided into four columns: policy, data, safety, and notice, with columns for responsible departments and supporting documents in each column.

tabs.label: policy
tabs.body: Check whether the purpose of the service complies with the provider's usage policy. The OpenAI usage policy includes automating critical decisions in sensitive areas without human review among the things users should not do. If our service touches a high-risk area, we also check this box to see if we have a human review point in place. Attached is a purpose statement and policy review memo as evidence.

tabs.label: data
tabs.body: Check what data is sent to the provider and under what conditions the data is stored. Abuse monitoring logs for the OpenAI API are retained by default for up to 30 days, and authorized customers can exclude customer content from these logs using Zero Data Retention or Modified Abuse Monitoring. The Gemini API retains prompts, context, and output for 55 days. Knowledge of the preservation conditions and records comparing them to our needs are proof.

tabs.label: safety
tabs.body: Check the presence of safety filters, setpoints, and evaluation results. If you have adjusted the thresholds, you should record what value you adjusted and why. The results of development and assurance evaluations, and whether or not they have gone through a red team are also items in this area. Attach evaluation records and safety settings history as proof.

tabs.label: notice
tabs.body: Check whether users are informed of the use of AI and, if so, where and with what text. Items to check include whether it is visible in a way that is noticeable, such as a conversation starter or a permanent badge on the screen, and whether it is designed to answer truthfully when asked if the user is human. Screen captures and response rule documents are attached as evidence.

screens.outro: Now that we've divided the areas, let's decide who approves and when to check again.

screens.title: Approval entity and re-inspection conditions
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Just because a review is complete does not mean approval for release is granted. There must be a separate entity, approval entity, that grants final release approval. By separating reviewers from approvers, we can reduce the number of The trap of checking what you have created yourself. Google's Responsible AI Toolkit recommends defining policies, designing safety, designing transparency, and designing security together, so approvers evaluate the results across all four areas at once. Additionally, after release, if events such as model replacement, changes to safety settings, connection to new data, incidents, or policy revisions occur, a new review must be conducted, and this process should be documented as Re-check conditions. The review is completed as Approvals and Records. Approval records should include the approver's name and date, the location of the review results that justified the approval, and if conditional approval is granted, also the remaining tasks and deadlines.

terms.tip: This person is responsible for reviewing the inspection results and authorizing the final release. It does not have to be the same person as the item manager; it is better to separate them.

terms.term: The trap of checking what you have created yourself
terms.tip: It is difficult for creators to see weaknesses in their work. Dividing the inspector and approver brings different perspectives.
This involves informing the service's approach through materials such as model cards. This is followed by an inspection of the upland area.
This is a pre-determined standard for re-examination when any changes occur. This standard prevents one-time inspection from being misunderstood as a permanent warranty.
The inspection is complete when it remains clear who approved it and on what basis it was approved.

screens.outro: Now that the components of the procedure have been gathered, let's look at the cases where items are missing through explanation.

screens.title: Explanation: If a problem arises due to missing inspection items
screens.lead: The instructor explains the counseling chatbot case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Example: A launch that only passes two areas
steps.body: The consultation chatbot has passed policy areas and safety assessments and been released. However, the data area of ​​the checklist was empty. No one checked what information was included in what customers entered or where and how that information was stored.

steps.title: Conditions for retaining sensitive information
steps.body: Customers may enter sensitive information such as social security numbers during consultation. Provider retains abuse monitoring logs for up to 30 days by default, which may contain customer content such as prompts and responses. Because we did not check this condition, we were unable to explain where and how much customer information was stored.

steps.title: There was a control option but it wasn't used.
steps.body: OpenAI advises that approved customers can exclude Customer Content from abuse monitoring logs with Zero Data Retention or Modified Abuse Monitoring. Although these options were in the provider documentation, they were not reviewed or requested because there were no data items on the checklist. Because these controls require prior approval and additional requirements, they should have been identified earlier to meet the launch schedule.

steps.title: Result: Post-explanation failure.
steps.body: When complaints were made, the company failed to explain retention periods and deletion responsibilities. The reviews and policies were great, but they didn't answer the first question customers ask: What happens to my information?

steps.title: lesson
steps.body: If one of the four areas is empty, the inspection is not complete. The fact that some areas are doing well does not make up for areas that are empty. This omission can be structurally prevented by fixing the form itself so that the four areas on the checklist are always visible.

screens.outro: Based on the causes of omission identified in the case, we will outline how to find the gaps in our checklist.

screens.title: Commentary: How to Judge the Completeness of a Checklist
screens.lead: Below is part of a team's checklist. When you select a highlighted passage, an explanation of how the instructor judged that space appears.

data.text: Policy Area: Purpose Definition Document Attached, Responsible Department Legal Team, There is proof. Data Area: Checked. Safety Area: Attach evaluation records and safety settings history, Responsible Department Security Team. Notification Area: Attached Conversation Start Phrase Capture, Responsible Department Service Planning Team. Approval: Signature field is empty. Re-inspection conditions: not stated.

marks.note: It only says that it has been confirmed, but there is no responsible department or supporting documents. Any space without evidence is judged to be incomplete and supplemented by writing down what was seen and confirmed. If this field is empty, it fails to describe retention periods and deletion responsibilities.

This space contains all items, responsible departments, and supporting documents. Use it as a standard to show what the completed Khan will look like. However, you should also read whether the evidence actually supports the item.

marks.span: Attach evaluation records and safety settings history
marks.note: There is two types of proof of the safe area: evaluation records and change history. If you map the multi-layered defense that Google documents refer to into different areas, filters, system directives, and evaluations each become a different layer of evidence.
Without an approver's signature or record of approval, no one has given permission for release. Even if the inspection is complete, the process is not complete without approval.

If no conditions are stated, the first inspection will be used as a permanent warranty. Conditions such as model replacement, safety settings change, new data connection, accident occurrence, policy revision, etc. should be required to be documented. It actually works if you specify who will notice changes and request rechecks for each condition. In conditions where only words are written and no one is in charge, no one moves even if actual changes occur.

screens.outro: I will organize the judgment criteria so far into one.

screens.title: The inspection is completed with approval and records.
screens.lead: Let's tie the content of this lesson into one design principle. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: The pre-launch inspection process answers four questions: The four areas of policy, data, safety, and notification answer what is checked, and the department responsible for each area answers who checks. How to know that something has been confirmed is determined by supporting documents, and whether it can be released is determined by the records of the approving entity.

One inspection is only a guarantee of the condition on the day of inspection. When the model changes, settings change, or new data is connected, the results of previous checks no longer describe the present. Therefore, the conditions under which re-inspection will be conducted must be written down in a document from the beginning.

When judging completeness, look for gaps. Among the four areas, check in order whether there are any empty areas, whether there is evidence in the box that only says ‘Confirmed’, whether there is an approval record, and whether there are re-check conditions written down. If even one is empty, the inspection is not yet complete.

To make this decision easier, pin the four areas and the approval and recheck condition boxes on the checklist form itself. If the form makes blank spaces visible, it can be checked using the same standards even if the person in charge changes. Each time a new risk is discovered, you add items to the form and record any changes, and the checklist grows with you.

Lastly, plan realistically how long the inspection process will take. Items that require prior approval from the provider, such as retention controls for data areas, are difficult to keep on schedule if started right before launch. If you figure out the time it takes for each inspection item and reflect it in the release schedule, you can reduce the occurrence of inspections being omitted because they are behind schedule.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: A checklist is a question-asking tool, not a disclaimer. It is more important to have a basis for each space than to fill it in.

checks.intro: Summarize the flow of the inspection procedure. Just place the four items in the correct order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Put the flow of completing pre-launch inspections in the correct order.
items: Check items in four areas: policy, data, safety, and notification.
Record responsible departments and supporting documents for each area
The person who approves the final release approves the inspection results.
Recheck if conditions such as model replacement or setting change occur.
checks.correctFeedback: We got the flow right from inspection to recording, approval, and re-inspection.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Rethink whether verification comes first, recording first, and when approval comes first.
checks.explain: The inspection is completed with approval and records, and conditions for re-inspection are set so that one inspection is not misunderstood as a permanent warranty.

checks.intro: This is an exercise in reading a checklist. Choose how you should judge the given space.
checks.q: The ‘Data’ column of the checklist only says ‘Confirmed’ and there is no responsible department or supporting documents. How should we judge?
options: Since the person in charge said it was confirmed, it is considered completed.
If the other three fields are filled out, the data field can be omitted.
Since there is no supporting document, it is considered incomplete and supplemented.
If there are re-check conditions, this field can be left empty.
checks.correctFeedback: We accurately applied the standard that confirmation without evidence is considered incomplete.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This judgment recognizes the box for which there is no evidence as complete.
checks.explain: A field that only says ‘Confirmed’ is incomplete without supporting documents. When data areas become empty, retention periods and deletion responsibilities cannot be accounted for after the fact.

wrong.1: If any of the four areas are empty, the inspection is incomplete.
wrong.3: Recheck conditions are separate items and cannot replace the blank spaces.

glossary.def: This is the process of verifying policies, data, safety, and notices before exposing them to customers. Items, responsibilities, evidence, and approvals must be grouped together as a set.
This is a checklist that includes inspection items, responsible departments, and supporting documents. It is more important to have a basis for each space than whether the space is filled.
This person is responsible for reviewing the inspection results and authorizing the final release. Separating yourself from itemized checkers reduces the pitfalls of self-checking.
This is a predetermined baseline for changes that need to be rechecked, such as replacing models, changing safety settings, or new data connections.

misconceptions.myth: One inspection just prior to launch is sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: As models, settings, and associated data change, previous checks do not account for the current one. You must set re-inspection conditions and re-inspect whenever changes occur.

misconceptions.myth: When the person in charge says it has been confirmed, the inspection is over.
misconceptions.fact: Words are not records. You must have responsible departments, supporting documentation, and approval records to prove that inspections were conducted even after an accident.

misconceptions.myth: As long as it passes the safety evaluation, it can be released.
misconceptions.fact: Safety is one of four areas: If the data's retention conditions, notices, and policy compliance are empty, the check is not complete even if the assessment has passed.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The inspection is completed with approval and records.
Items should cover all four areas: Policy, Data, Safety, and Notices.
Separate inspectors and approvers and support verification with supporting documentation.
Re-inspection conditions must be established so that one inspection is not misunderstood as a permanent warranty.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which box on our checklist is empty for proof? Think of each of the four areas and find the weakest one.
